briefing.focus: Fairway-finder day. 139 slope, narrow and tree-lined — the mini driver and 2-iron are your scoring clubs off the tee, and bogey is never an emergency here.

sections.t: The course in one paragraph
sections.b: Mungeam design (2004) carved into a hillside: 6,935 yards, par 71, rating 73.7 / slope 139 from the tips — the longest, toughest, best-kept muni in Westchester. Narrow fairways lined with trees and fescue, elevated tees AND elevated greens, a few blind shots, and almost no flat lies. Front nine is an accuracy exam; back nine wants length and short game. Play the tees that match a 6,300–6,500 game, not the tips — the slope is real.

sections.t: Off the tee — your bag is built for this place
sections.b: This is exactly why you carry the r7 Mini and the 2-iron. Blind or squeezed landing area (the 2nd is famously tight, the 7th is a beast): mini driver (~220) or 2-iron (~205) and walk to the fairway. Save the Stealth 2 for the open, longer back-nine holes where the extra 15 yards matters. One rule all day: on any tee shot you can't fully see, take the club you'd bet $100 finds short grass.

sections.t: The lies are the hidden test
sections.b: Hillside course = sidehill everything. Ball above your feet wants to go LEFT — with your strong lofts, take one less club and aim right edge. Ball below feet pushes right; widen the stance and swing smooth. Uphill approach: club UP, always — elevated greens reject anything short and roll it 20 yards back down the hill. Short-siding yourself here is the double-bogey machine; center of every green is a genuinely good shot.

sections.t: Wedges & lay-ups
sections.b: When you punch out or lay up, do it to YOUR numbers: 95 (full 56°) or 108 (full 50°) — not 'as far as possible' into an awkward half-shot from a sloped lie. On uphill wedges into elevated greens, the ball lands steep and stops fast: fly it to the flag.

sections.t: Greens — first real test for the DF3i
sections.b: Reviewers call them tour-fast. Perfect debut for the zero-torque: your job is speed only, the face is handled. Lag ladder mindset from 25+ feet — die everything into the 6-foot circle. Spend the first three greens calibrating pace, and on breaking putts play extra break with dying speed. Keep the low-through-impact feel from the gate drill: that is still your one open fault, and fast greens punish a popped stroke worst.

sections.t: Logistics & scoring mindset
sections.b: Extremely hilly — take the cart, save the legs for the back nine. July heat means carries play a touch longer (load the weather tile at the first tee — the ladder's Today column does the math). Target: doubles are the enemy, not bogeys. Count them; fewer than three doubles on a 139 slope is a won day. Log the round in Coach after — score, putts, and what bit you — and I'll debrief it against this plan.

briefing.focus: Conventional vs. left-hand-low vs. claw — decided by makes and miss direction, not feel. One stage at a time.

sections.t: Why your right hand is the suspect
sections.b: For a right-handed putter, the trail hand is the strong, dominant one — under pressure it wants to rotate and flip the face closed through impact, and a closed face is a pull left. That is literally what Session 1's frame-by-frame showed: toe-over rotation, varying rep to rep. Both alternative grips exist to take that rotation out of the stroke. The DF3i already removes most of the need — this experiment measures what's left.

sections.t: The three contenders
sections.b: CONVENTIONAL (reverse overlap): handle in the palms, palms parallel to the face, thumbs down the Press Pistol's flat front, pressure 3/10, right palm 'along for the ride.' LEFT-HAND-LOW: lead hand below trail — levels the shoulders and turns the stroke into a shoulder-rocked pendulum; the structural fix, and a natural pair with a straight SBST stroke. CLAW: normal left hand, right hand in a pencil/saw hold — the surgical 'delete the right hand' move; smallest change, shines inside 10 feet.

sections.t: Stage 0 — baseline the conventional grip FIRST (weeks 1–2)
sections.b: You just changed the two biggest levers (zero-torque head, lie). Roll the DF3i with your normal grip for two weeks: one 20-ball 5-footer test per week, tapped into the Putting Lab with miss directions. GATE: 2 or fewer left misses per 20 in both weeks → conventional wins, experiment over, don't add complexity to a solved problem. 3+ lefts in either week → advance to Stage 1.

sections.t: Stage 1 — the head-to-head (only if the gate trips)
sections.b: Practice-green session: alternate 10-ball blocks from 5 feet — conventional, LHL, claw, then repeat (60 balls, two blocks each). Log every block in the Decisions 10-ball tester named 'DF3i · conventional', 'DF3i · LHL', 'DF3i · claw' with miss pattern notes. Then add the lag check: 5 balls from 30 feet with each grip — average leave distance matters as much as makes, because alternative grips usually tax distance feel first. Two separate sessions minimum before any verdict.

sections.t: Stage 2 — commit and groove
sections.b: Winner = most makes + fewest left misses across all blocks, with a lag leave you can live with. Commit to it for 3 full weeks before re-judging (every grip change feels bad for two weeks — that's adaptation, not information). Hybrid option is legitimate: conventional for lag, claw inside 10 feet, if the blocks split that way. Film one face-on session with the winner so the early-lift verdict lands on the final setup.

sections.t: The setup constants — same for all three grips
sections.b: These never change during the experiment, so the grip is the only variable. BALL POSITION: one to two ball-widths inside your lead (left) heel — forward of center, so the DF3i meets the ball just past the low point with a slight upstroke for true roll (ball too far back = downward strike = the hop-and-skid your old thin contact hinted at). EYES: directly over the ball or a hair inside the line — run the nose-drop test once to set it (drop a ball from the bridge of your nose at address; it should land on the ball or just inside). STANCE: feet shoulder-width, knees soft, weight 55/45 favoring the lead side, and dead still — the stroke moves, the body doesn't. DISTANCE FROM BALL: arms hang straight down from the shoulders, no reaching — this also keeps the sole flat (the toe-up aim-left problem lives here). ALIGNMENT: square the face to your line FIRST, then build the stance around the face. PRESS: none added — the Press Pistol 2° has the forward lean built in; hands sit even with the ball.

sections.t: Grip 1 · Conventional (reverse overlap) — the exact hold
sections.b: LEFT HAND first, at the top: the handle runs up your LIFELINE (the crease between thumb pad and heel pad), NOT across the fingers like a full-swing grip — this locks the wrist. Left thumb flat, straight down the Press Pistol's flat front. RIGHT HAND below it: same palm placement — handle up the lifeline, right thumb flat down the front — so both PALMS FACE EACH OTHER, parallel to the putter face. They now work as one unit: if the palms oppose, the face can't rotate without both wrists agreeing. FINISH: lift your left index finger and lay it OVER the fingers of the right hand (across the pinky and ring finger) — that's the reverse overlap, and it further handcuffs the right wrist. Pressure 3/10, both hands. Feel: the back of the left hand IS the putter face — swing it at the target; the right palm just mirrors.

sections.t: Grip 2 · Left-hand-low — the exact hold
sections.b: Everything mirrors: RIGHT HAND goes at the TOP now — handle up the right lifeline, right thumb flat down the front. LEFT HAND below it — handle up the left lifeline, left thumb down the front, palms opposing as always. OVERLAP: lay your right index finger over the fingers of the left hand (the mirror of reverse overlap). CRITICAL CHECKS: your shoulders should feel — and be — LEVEL at address (that's the whole point; the normal grip tilts the right shoulder down), and your LEFT wrist stays flat and leads the stroke like a paddle; the left hand going low turns your lead side into the engine and demotes the right hand to a passenger. Expect it to feel alien for two weeks and expect lag to suffer first — that's why the 30-foot check is in the protocol.

sections.t: Grip 3 · Claw — the exact hold
sections.b: LEFT HAND: identical to conventional — top of the grip, up the lifeline, thumb down the front. This hand now does ALL the holding. RIGHT HAND: rotate it so the palm faces YOUR BODY (not the target), then hold the grip like a PENCIL — thumb pad resting on the back of the handle, the first two fingertips lying on the front/top. The handle sits in the notch between thumb and index finger. Pressure 2/10 — the right hand is a fairing, not a motor; it physically cannot rotate the face from that position, which is the entire trick. Right elbow drifts slightly away from your side — let it. Variation if the pencil feels twitchy: the SAW — same idea but all four right fingertips lie across the front of the grip like holding a saw handle. Either counts as 'claw' in the blocks; pick one and keep it.

The two real misses share a signature: both balls DIED at the hole. One settled an inch to the pull side, one hung on the near-left lip. Clips end at arrival, so 'vanish + full-length return' = make is the scoring rule.

sections.t: The one connection: laid-off top + stalled hips are the same story
sections.b: When the club gets across the line / laid off at the top (shaft pointing right of target, trail elbow drifting behind you), the downswing has to re-route the club to save the shot. The most common save is the hips SLIDING toward the target and the chest hanging back — which is precisely the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' feeling. So we don't chase two separate fixes: clean up the top so the hips don't have to bail you out, and train the hips to CLEAR (rotate open) instead of slide. Fix the cause, the symptom follows.

sections.t: What the film showed (both clubs, Jul 26)
sections.b: GOOD, protect it: full coil, head behind the ball (driver), lower-body-led transition on both, and a balanced held finish. WEDGE bonus: spine angle stayed, you covered the ball — a proper descending strike. TO FIX: (1) slightly across-the-line top on BOTH clubs — one feel fixes both; (2) driver hips look to slide level through impact instead of clearing up-and-around. sections.t: Fix 1 · Clean up the top (trail elbow in front)
sections.b: FEEL: at the top, the trail (right) elbow points more DOWN at the ground and stays in FRONT of your trail-hip seam, keeping the club a hair more in front of your chest. Right now the elbow drifts behind you, which lays the shaft off. DRILL — Split-hand / trail-arm-only: make slow half-swings feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot; pause at the top and check the shaft points AT the target line, not right of it. Mirror or a phone on a tripod DTL at the top confirms it. 10 slow reps before you hit balls.

sections.t: Fix 2 · Clear the hips, don't slide them
sections.b: FEEL: from the top, the lead (left) hip clears BACK and UP — belt buckle turning left and rotating open — while your chest stays over the ball a beat longer. Not a slide toward the target; a turn around a post. This is where your speed and your 'through contact' consistency live. DRILLS: (a) Trail-foot-back / step-through: hit half wedges stepping the trail foot back through impact — forces rotation over slide. (b) Lead-hip-to-the-wall: set up with your lead hip a few inches off a wall/bag; on the downswing the hip should clear so it just brushes back and up, not bump forward into it. (c) Chair/impact-bag: feel the trail glute fire and the hips deepen (not thrust toward the ball) so you don't early-extend. 2–3 sets of 10 each, twice a week.

briefing.focus: Your WINNERSPIRIT Miracle 201 is the perfect home tool for the two things the Jul 26 film flagged: sequencing (hips lead) and releasing THROUGH contact instead of losing it. This is the standing at-home practice plan. Pairs with the Swing Focus plan.

sections.t: How the tool talks to you (read first)
sections.b: The Miracle 201 is a weighted (~550g), whippy carbon/glass-fiber trainer with TWO feedback channels. (1) THE CLICK: a slider fires an audible click at the point of maximum speed in your swing — WHERE you hear it tells you WHEN you're releasing. (2) THE SPEED DIAL: adjustable from ~15–50 m/s (≈34–111 mph); it sets how much speed is needed to trigger the click. Turn it DOWN for tempo work, UP to demand more clubhead speed or simulate a longer club. Because the shaft is heavy and flexible, you physically cannot rush it — it forces you to load and wait, which is exactly the medicine for your quick, across-the-line top.

sections.t: Setup & safety — every session
sections.b: Space: ~8 ft clear all around and a high ceiling (garage, basement with clearance, or backyard). Never near people, lights, or a TV. Hold it with your normal CONVENTIONAL grip and your real posture — this only transfers if the setup matches your actual swing. WARM UP FIRST: 20–30 slow, smooth swings before anything hard — at 550g it's heavier than your driver and a cold max swing is how you tweak a back or oblique. Do a few swings LEFT-handed too (opposite of normal) each session — it balances the body and builds the anti-rotation muscles that protect you.

sections.t: Drill 1 · Tempo & sequencing — the load-and-wait (core)
sections.b: Dial LOW. Make smooth 3:1 swings and FEEL the shaft bend and lag behind your hands at the top — if you snatch from the top it flails and clicks early/weak. Count 'one-and-… two': long patient load back, unhurried transition, then let it sling. This directly rewires the 'great at the top but quick coming down' pattern. 2 sets of 10, both directions. This is the most important drill on the list — do it every session.

sections.t: Drill 2 · Impact timing — make the CLICK fire PAST the ball
sections.b: This one targets your exact complaint: 'lose it through contact.' GOAL: the click should crack at the BOTTOM of the arc — at or just PAST your lead leg — not up in the downswing. An EARLY click = casting / throwing the release away before impact (all your speed spent above the ball). Keep the wrists hinged and let the head release LATE so the click fires down by where the ball would be. 3 sets of 8. Listen every rep and adjust until the click consistently lives at/after the bottom.

sections.t: Drill 3 · Transition & hips-lead (ties to Swing Focus)
sections.b: From the top, start down with the LOWER BODY — feel the lead hip clear BACK and UP while the trainer's head still lags behind. Because the head is heavy and slow to catch up, it exaggerates the hips-lead-hands feeling you need. If you spin the shoulders/arms first, the click comes early and weak — instant feedback that you cast. Do this right after the wall / trail-foot-back drills in your Swing Focus plan so the feel carries over. 2 sets of 8.

sections.t: Drill 4 · Top-of-swing check — kill the laid-off shaft
sections.b: Slow reps to a PAUSE at the top. Feel the trail (right) elbow point down and stay IN FRONT of your trail-hip seam — the whippy shaft makes an across-the-line/laid-off top feel obviously 'stuck' and off-plane, which a normal club hides. Check in a mirror or a phone on a tripod that the shaft points at the target line, not right of it. 10 slow reps, no speed — this is a position drill.

sections.t: Drill 5 · Speed sets (separate days)
sections.b: Dial UP. After a full warm-up: all-out swings for pure speed — at higher dial settings the click ONLY fires if you genuinely accelerate through the bottom. Protocol: 3 sets of 5 MAX-effort swings with full rest between sets (this is nervous-system/speed work — quality over quantity, never grind it into cardio). Throw in a few non-dominant-side swings. Benchmark: the highest dial setting you can consistently trigger — track it over weeks and watch it climb.

sections.t: Weekly plan & what to log
sections.b: 2–3 short sessions/week, 10–15 min each — and DON'T max out every time: alternate a TEMPO/TIMING day (Drills 1–4, low dial) with a SPEED day (Drill 5, high dial). Pre-round: 15–20 easy swings as a dynamic warm-up and tempo primer. Log in Coach: the dial setting you can reliably trigger, and whether the click is firing at/past the ball yet. Next time you film at the sim we'll check whether the later release and hips-lead carried into the real swing.

briefing.focus: A checkpoint map of WHERE the body goes — feet, knees, hips, spine, hands, head — from address to finish, so you can freeze each spot in a mirror or on video and match it. Built to answer 'where am I supposed to be?' — especially the hips (see the last two sections). RH references: LEAD = left, TRAIL = right.

sections.t: How to use this
sections.b: Don't try to hit all of these at once — that's paralysis. Pick ONE checkpoint per session, rehearse it slowly in a mirror (face-on) and on a down-the-line phone clip, then hit a few balls letting it happen. Positions are a map, not a swing thought for over the ball. Everything below is for a right-handed golfer: LEAD side = left, TRAIL side = right.

sections.t: 1 · Address — the setup everything else depends on
sections.b: FEET: shoulder-width for irons (insides of the heels about under your armpits), a touch wider for driver. Flare the LEAD foot out ~20–30° — this pre-clears room for the hips to turn through later. WEIGHT: 50/50 for irons, balanced on the arches (not toes, not heels); driver slightly on the trail side (~55/45). KNEES: soft athletic flex, like the top of a light squat — not locked, not deep. HIPS: hinge from the hip SOCKETS, not the waist — push your butt back like you're closing a car door with it. Pelvis neutral, hips level, small natural arch in the low back. SPINE/CHEST: tilt forward from that hinge so your chest is over the balls of your feet, plus a slight trail-shoulder-lower tilt (natural, since the trail hand sits lower on the grip). ARMS/HANDS: let the arms hang straight down from the shoulders — hands roughly under your chin, over your shoelaces. Irons: slight shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh. Driver: hands level with the ball. HEAD: steady, eyes down, chin UP off your chest so the lead shoulder can turn under it. BALL: driver off the lead heel; irons center to just right of center (your Golf Mind note).

sections.t: 2 · Takeaway — halfway back (club parallel to the ground)
sections.b: Move it back in ONE PIECE — hands, arms and chest turn together, no early wrist roll. FEET/KNEES: quiet; weight just starting to press into the trail heel. HIPS: barely rotating — the TRAIL hip is turning BEHIND you, not sliding out over the trail foot (that slide is a sway). CHECKPOINT: shaft parallel to the target line, toe pointing up, hands over the trail thigh, lead arm straight and still across the chest.

sections.t: 3 · Top of the backswing
sections.b: FEET: pressure loaded into the trail heel and instep; lead heel can stay down or lift slightly — either is fine. KNEES: the TRAIL knee HOLDS its address flex — if it straightens, you've swayed/stood up. HIPS: turned ~45° so your belt buckle points right of the ball, and you feel LOADED into the trail glute — like you're sitting into that right hip. Trail hip should still be inside the trail foot (outside it = sway). SPINE: same tilt you set at address, unchanged. SHOULDERS: turned ~90°, lead shoulder under the chin, upper back to the target — shoulders turn about twice as much as the hips (that gap is your coil). ARMS/HANDS: lead arm comfortably straight; TRAIL ELBOW points more DOWN at the ground and stays IN FRONT of the trail-hip seam (your working feel); shaft points at / parallel to the target line — not laid off across it. HEAD: still behind the ball, quiet.

sections.t: 4 · Transition — how the downswing STARTS (your problem spot)
sections.b: The ORDER is the whole game, and it runs ground-up WHILE the club is still finishing the backswing. (1) FEET/PRESSURE FIRST: press down into the LEAD foot — feel pressure move to the lead heel/instep. (2) HIPS SECOND: the LEAD hip then CLEARS — it rotates open (turns left) and back behind you and UP — while (3) the arms and club simply DROP into the slot (this is exactly your one-arm feel). You are NOT shoving the hips toward the target; you're turning them out of the way so the arms have room to fall. TRAIL SIDE: trail heel starts to lift, trail knee kicks in toward the lead knee. CHECKPOINT (down-the-line): when your hands reach hip height, the shaft should point at or just outside the ball and your hips are ALREADY opening. If the hands get to the ball before the hips have turned, you cast.

sections.t: 5 · Impact — the position all of it is for
sections.b: FEET: ~80–90% of pressure on the LEAD foot; trail foot up on the inside of the toe. LEAD LEG: straightening / 'posting up' — this extension pulls the hips up and around and is a big chunk of the speed you lose when you slide instead. HIPS: OPEN ~35–45° to the target — belt buckle already pointing LEFT of the ball, lead hip HIGH and behind you. SPINE/CHEST: still tilted, chest 'covering' the ball; for irons and wedges you stay DOWN through it. HANDS: ahead of the ball for irons (shaft lean, hands over the lead thigh); level for driver so you catch it slightly on the up. HEAD: still behind the ball, eyes down. This is the money frame — most of the checkpoints above exist only to get you here.

sections.t: 6 · Follow-through & finish
sections.b: Keep rotating — the belt buckle turns from left-of-the-ball all the way to facing the target and past it. FEET: fully onto the lead foot, trail foot balanced on the toe with the laces to the target. HIPS: fully cleared and open, LEAD LEG tall and straight. CHEST: faces the target, then left of it. ARMS: extend down the line just after impact (the 'chase'), then fold up to a tall, balanced finish. Test: if you can HOLD the finish for 3 seconds without falling off balance, your sequence and weight shift were good.

sections.t: 7 · The HIPS in plain terms — SLIDE vs CLEAR (read twice)
sections.b: You're unsure here, so plainly: coming down, the hips can do two different things. A SLIDE is the hips moving SIDEWAYS toward the target — the belt buckle stays pointing at the ball, the hips stay 'closed,' and your upper body hangs back to counterbalance. That is the 'great at the top, lose it through contact' miss: no speed, hands flip to square the face, thin or fat strikes. A CLEAR (what you want) is the hips ROTATING — the lead hip turns back behind you and up as the lead leg straightens, so the belt buckle points LEFT of the ball at impact. THREE IMAGES that make it click: (a) There's a wall just behind your lead butt cheek — clearing = that cheek moves BACK to the wall, not toward the target. (b) You're standing in a barrel — you can TURN inside it but you can't slide out of it. (c) Pull your lead back pocket around behind you and up. Note: a SMALL lateral shift is real and necessary — but it happens in the FEET (pressure to the lead foot), and THEN the hips turn. Feet shift, hips spin — never the whole pelvis sliding as one block.

sections.t: 8 · How to groove it (feel beats positions)
sections.b: Positions are for the mirror; feels are for hitting. briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits off the front foot — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination actually costs you, why it lands squarely on the one putting fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma.

sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the DF3i meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.

sections.t: The second cost — the pull
sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b: Hanging back leaves the hands behind the ball through impact. Hands behind = the wrists want to save it = a flick. That flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. The DF3i's zero-torque head has buried that miss on film — but hands-behind is the one setup that can wake it up.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b: Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold. (1) STERNUM at or just ahead of the ball. (2) HANDS level with or a touch ahead of the ball at impact — never behind it. (3) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the DF3i is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. (4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.

sections.t: Settle it with data, not opinion
sections.b: A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current weight-back feel. Block B: 55/45 lead, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: check shaft lean at impact and where the head bottoms out relative to the ball.

sections.t: One thing in your favor
sections.b: The DF3i at 34" is zero-torque and heavy in the head — it squares itself and it wants to be swung, not steered. You can bias a touch more forward than feels natural without losing the feel you like. This putter absorbs the change better than a blade would.

sections.t: The setup, your words
sections.b: Ball position off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked right ON the ball. Normal address. Forward press right before contact, then putt. This supersedes the weight-back feel that started the conversation — the low point question is answered.

sections.t: Why the chest reference beats the foot reference
sections.b: You landed on 'left breast' rather than 'front heel,' and that's the better cue — keep it. The arc of a shoulder-rocked stroke is centered on your STERNUM, not your feet. Referencing the ball to your chest points it at the thing that actually governs the low point. Foot reference drifts every time your stance width changes by an inch; the chest reference doesn't. In putting posture those two land in roughly the same place anyway, so you've lost nothing and gained a cue that travels.

sections.t: Weight stacked on the ball — what that buys
sections.b: Pressure over the ball puts the sternum over or a whisker behind it, which pins the arc's bottom right where it belongs: at or just behind the ball, so the DF3i is a hair ascending at contact. That's the true-roll window. It's also why the setup 'feels good' — a pinned low point is what a repeatable strike feels like from the inside.

sections.t: The forward press — a TRIGGER, not a position
sections.b: This is a change from the static 'hands even, no press' note, and it's a legitimate one — because a press before contact does a different job than press held at address. Its purpose is to break inertia and start the stroke rhythmically instead of from a dead, frozen stop. Crenshaw, Nicklaus, half the great putters ever. Your tempo was a documented fault once (~1:1, fixed to 2.4:1 by the One-Two drill) — a press trigger is genuine maintenance for that.

sections.t: The one rule for the press
sections.b: SAME SIZE, EVERY TIME. The press changes the shaft lean, the shaft lean changes the effective loft, and the loft changes how far the ball rolls. A press that varies putt to putt is a loft that varies putt to putt — which is a PACE that varies putt to putt, and pace is the only fault still open on your card. Make it small, make it identical, and move it along the target line rather than hinging the wrists. The DF3i's zero-torque head protects the face; it can't protect you from a press that changes size.

sections.t: The routine as you described it
sections.b: 1) Line it up — read, aim the FACE first. 2) Set feet and hands, normal address. 3) Look at the hole. 4) Look at the aiming spot. 5) Look at the ball. 6) Forward press. 7) Putt. Structurally sound: face aimed before the stance gets built, an intermediate spot for line, one clear trigger to start it. Keep it brisk — three looks is the most you want before you go stale over the ball.

sections.t: THE GAP — nothing in this routine sets pace
sections.b: Read the seven steps again and ask what any of them does about how HARD you hit it. Nothing. Every step is aimed at LINE — the read, the face, the spot, the ball. And line is the part of your putting that's already settled: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. The one thing still broken is pace — lags short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, both Stage-0 misses dying at the hole. Your routine has no pace step in it at all.

sections.t: The fix — one rehearsal stroke, eyes on the hole
sections.b: Add ONE practice stroke between step 3 and step 4, made while LOOKING AT THE HOLE, that rehearses the actual LENGTH of stroke the putt needs. This is the single most reliable distance-control device there is: your eyes calibrate stroke size to distance far better than your conscious mind estimates it. Then look at the spot, look at the ball, press, go — pace is already loaded, and the last look is line. One rehearsal, not three.

sections.t: Worth testing on lags
sections.b: On anything past ~25 feet, try keeping your eyes ON THE HOLE through the stroke instead of returning them to the ball. It feels absurd and it is remarkably effective for distance — the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. Test it as a block, not mid-round: 10 lags eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, measure the spread of stopping points. Same measurement protocol as the weight A/B.

That was written about the static address position and it's still true there — but it now sits awkwardly next to a deliberate press trigger. They're compatible (address neutral, press to start), just say so in the note so future-you doesn't read it as a contradiction.

Everything here is aimed at the single root cause the Jul 26 film found: an across-the-line top that forces a re-route, which shows up as sliding hips and the over-the-top slice. sections.t: The architecture — two zones
sections.b: BEHIND THE BALL is where every decision and every rehearsal happens. AT THE BALL is execution only — no thinking, no adjusting, no second guesses. In the full swing you're not calibrating magnitude, you're calibrating SHAPE and SEQUENCE — those transfer fine from behind the ball, and the commitment you buy is worth more. sections.t: 1 · Decide (behind the ball)
sections.b: Lie, wind, number, and where the trouble ISN'T. Then pick a SPECIFIC target — a tree, a bunker lip, a chimney — never 'the fairway'. DRIVER: aim the CENTER of the fairway, because your start line tends to pull left and center-aim leaves you room. Commit to ONE shape and say it out loud in your head. sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the DF3i meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.

sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.

sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. briefing.focus: A pre-shot routine built around YOUR pattern, not a generic one. Everything here is aimed at the single root cause the Jul 26 film found: an across-the-line top that forces a re-route, which shows up as sliding hips and the over-the-top slice. The routine's job is to stop you re-routing — and re-routing is something you do OVER the ball, so the routine gets the deciding done before you're standing there.

sections.t: The architecture — two zones
sections.b: BEHIND THE BALL is where every decision and every rehearsal happens. AT THE BALL is execution only — no thinking, no adjusting, no second guesses. This is the opposite of what we locked for putting, and deliberately so: in putting you rehearse beside the ball because stroke SIZE has to transfer exactly. In the full swing you're not calibrating magnitude, you're calibrating SHAPE and SEQUENCE — those transfer fine from behind the ball, and the commitment you buy is worth more. Different problem, different answer.

sections.t: 1 · Decide (behind the ball)
sections.b: Lie, wind, number, and where the trouble ISN'T. Then pick a SPECIFIC target — a tree, a bunker lip, a chimney — never 'the fairway'. DRIVER: aim the CENTER of the fairway, because your start line tends to pull left and center-aim leaves you room. Commit to ONE shape and say it out loud in your head. Then stop deciding — anything you reconsider later gets reconsidered over the ball, which is exactly where your swing falls apart.

sections.t: 2 · Rehearse (behind the ball, facing the target)
sections.b: ONE rehearsal swing. Not three. Feel the trail (right) elbow drop DOWN and stay IN FRONT of your trail-hip seam — that is the whole fix, and it's the one that repairs the top, the hips and the slice together. If the last swing felt across the line, make this a TRAIL-ARM-ONLY rehearsal instead: one hand, slow, feeling the drop into the slot. That's the feel that's been landing for you with the one-handed Miracle 201, and a normal club held trail-arm-only is a fine stand-in on the course.

sections.t: 3 · Aim (stepping in)
sections.b: Pick an intermediate spot a foot or two ahead of the ball on your start line. Set the CLUBFACE to that spot FIRST, then build the stance around the face — never the other way round. Feet shoulder-width (a touch wider for driver), lead foot flared 20–30° so the hips have somewhere to go. Ball off the lead heel for driver, center to just right of center for irons. Weight 50/50 irons, ~55/45 trail side for driver. Hinge from the hip SOCKETS, chin UP off the chest so the lead shoulder can turn under it.

sections.t: 4 · Go (no decisions left)
sections.b: One look at the target. One look back to the ball. Then a TRIGGER — a small waggle or a kick of the trail knee. Never start a swing from a frozen stand; a static start is where the snatch comes from, and the snatch is what lays the club off. Count it: 'one-and-… two.' Long patient load, unhurried transition, 3:1. Then hold the finish for THREE SECONDS. If you can't hold it, the sequence or the weight shift was off — that's free feedback on every single swing.

sections.t: The one-thought rule
sections.b: ONE swing thought at a time. If you have two, you have none. Yours is the trail elbow — down and in front of the trail-hip seam. Everything else on your card (hip clearance, the slice, the laid-off top) is downstream of that one feel, which is exactly why you don't need a second thought. Rotate a different thought in only when the film says the root has moved.

sections.t: The step-off rule
sections.b: If anything feels wrong once you're over the ball — alignment, the number, a gust, a stray thought — STEP OFF and restart from behind the ball. Do not fix it standing there. Over-the-ball corrections are precisely how a re-route gets built into a swing, and re-routing is your documented fault. Stepping off costs eight seconds; a re-route costs the shot.

sections.t: Under pressure — longer, not shorter
sections.b: Your own note: the straight ball comes from a LONGER, fuller swing; a tighter, shorter swing turns into a cut, and when that goes wrong the miss is a PUSH-SLICE. Pressure makes everyone shorten and steer, so this is the rule that needs saying out loud before a tee shot that matters — when in doubt, commit to MORE swing, never less. Steering is the re-route wearing a disguise.

sections.t: Warm-up primer — before the first tee
sections.b: A few slow ONE-HANDED reps with the Miracle 201, or trail-arm-only with a club, feeling the elbow lead down into the slot. Then blend into two-hand swings. This is your documented working feel — prime it before the round rather than hunting for it on the 4th hole. And keep the routine's beat count identical from the range to the 18th; a routine that shortens under pressure isn't a routine.

sections.t: Wedges — one addition
sections.b: Everything above holds, plus: partial distances come from a CONTROLLED length and flight, not a full send with a soft grip. Choke down and hit the control shot. Your ladder off the 44° PW: 60°→80 · 56°→95 · 50°→108 · PW→122. Decide the NUMBER behind the ball like any other shot — the wedge swing on film is already good (spine held, ball-first, covering it); it's the distance decision that needs the routine.

briefing.focus: Scramble, not stroke play. Your job is to be the team's SECOND ball — when someone's already safe, swing free and go at the flag. And on every lay-up, leave the team one of YOUR numbers (122 · 108 · 95 · 80), never a 70-yard guess.

sections.t: The course in one paragraph
sections.b: Beekman Golf Course, Hopewell Junction NY (11 Country Club Rd) — a 1964 Cortlandt Fish public 27-holer in the Berkshire foothills where they rise out of the Hudson Valley, about an hour's drive for you. Three nines — HIGHLAND (3,142 yds, par 36, ~124 slope), VALLEY (2,952, par 35, ~118), TACONIC (3,125, par 36, ~126) — played in three 18-hole pairings between 6,485 and 6,532 yards. Zoysia fairways, which is the detail worth knowing: zoysia sits the ball UP on a tight, firm cushion, so contact is clean and there's less grab than the bent/poa you're used to. Reviews are consistent — well-kept greens, all three nines hilly, and it doesn't drain well, so wet spots after rain.

sections.t: Find out which two nines you're playing
sections.b: Ask at check-in, because the three nines are genuinely different golf courses. TACONIC is the hardest: narrowest fairways and the water — the par-5 6th has a pond fronting the green, which in a scramble is a decision hole, not a hero hole. HIGHLAND climbs over 500 feet to a panorama of Stormville Mountain: elevation change on nearly every shot, blind or semi-blind looks, and the yardage on the sprinkler head is a starting point, not the answer. VALLEY is the gentlest and flattest of the three — that's your birdie nine, and a scramble team that only pars the Valley holes has already lost the tournament.

sections.t: Scramble math — where teams actually win
sections.b: You don't win a scramble by avoiding doubles; the format erases those for you. You win it by converting the 5–7 genuinely gettable holes and by never wasting a hole where all four of you miss. So the whole game is about SEQUENCING: get one ball safe, then let everyone else be aggressive off that safety net. The single biggest error you'll see all day is the team's last hitter playing conservatively when a ball is already in the fairway — that shot is completely free, and a free shot played safe is a shot thrown away.

sections.t: Your role off the tee
sections.b: You have the perfect scramble bag for this: mini driver (~220) and the KING TEC 2-iron (~205) for when a ball simply has to be in the short grass, and the Stealth 2 for when one already is. Rule for the day: if nobody is safe yet, hit the club you'd bet $100 finds the fairway — on Taconic's tight holes and Highland's blind ones, that's the mini or the 2-iron, and nobody on your team will ever complain about a ball in play. If someone IS safe, take the driver and take the whole thing on. Your own note from the swing plan applies double here: the straight one comes from a LONGER, fuller swing; steering it is what turns it into the push-slice. In a scramble you have permission to make the fullest swing you own.

sections.t: Approaches — the lay-up is the shot that scores
sections.b: This is the biggest edge you personally bring, and almost nobody uses it. In a scramble you CHOOSE the yardage for the next shot. On any par 5 you're laying up on — including Taconic's 6th over the water — pick the ball that leaves a full 95 (56°) or a full 108 (50°), not the one that's 18 yards closer and leaves a nervy three-quarter 70-yarder. Same on a punch-out. Your ladder off the 44° PW: PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80. Say the number out loud when the team is choosing the ball — it's the most useful sentence you can contribute all day. On approaches themselves: first player in plays to the CENTER of the green, everyone after that fires at the flag. Uphill into these hillside greens, club UP; anything short rolls back down to you.

sections.t: The hill, the lies, and your free club-length
sections.b: All three nines are hilly, so you'll get very few flat lies — except that a scramble hands you a club-length of relief (confirm no-closer-to-the-hole at check-in). USE IT properly: don't just drop it where it's convenient, walk it to the flattest stance and the best ANGLE into the flag, and get out of any divot or wet spot. When you're stuck with a slope: ball above your feet turns it LEFT — with your strong lofts take one less and aim at the right edge; ball below the feet leaks right, so widen the stance and swing smooth. On the Highland especially, trust the elevation over the number.

sections.t: Putting — the whole team's read is yours to use
sections.b: Best sequencing: whoever's least confident putts first and the best putter goes last, so the last ball has watched three balls take the line. Everyone marks the spot and putts from it. Two things that win scrambles on the green: the early putters should get the ball PAST the hole so the team learns the break and the speed — a putt left short teaches nothing — and the last putter plays the read that the first three just paid for. For you specifically: the DF3i handles the face, so your job is pace, and the routine still runs on every putt, including the 3-footer after a teammate has already stuffed it close. Your signature miss is left on the short ones, and 'gimme' tap-ins in a scramble are exactly where a stroke gets loose.

sections.t: The opening hole — you have data on this
sections.b: Wianno told you the truth in numbers: across five opening holes you went 6, 6, 5, 4, 6 — SEVEN over par on five holes, and never a par on the first hole of a front nine. That's a not-warmed-up problem, not a swing problem, and you're driving an hour to a 7 AM-ish start. Get there early enough for the warm-up primer off the swing plan: a few slow ONE-HANDED reps (Miracle 201 or trail-arm-only), feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot, then blend to two-handed swings. Then five minutes on the putting green for pace only — zoysia surrounds and well-kept greens mean you want the speed calibrated before the first putt counts for four people.

sections.t: Confirm these at check-in
sections.b: Scramble formats vary and the details change your strategy: (1) is there a MINIMUM DRIVES rule — most events require each player's tee shot be used two or three times? If so, bank yours early on the wide holes rather than discovering on 17 that you owe two. (2) Net or gross, and how team handicap is figured. (3) Whether they're selling mulligans/skins — buy them for the tightest tee shots, not the first hole. (4) Cart path only? On a course this hilly, that changes club selection every hole. (5) Which nines, and shotgun or tee times.

sections.t: Mindset for the day
sections.b: Early August, hilly, an hour in the car first — take the cart, drink more than you think, and load the weather tile at the first tee so the ladder's Today column adjusts your carries for the heat. This is the one round all year where your worst shot literally does not exist, so the risk-management instincts that serve you in stroke play are mostly wrong here: be the guy who takes on the flag once a teammate is safe. Log it in Coach afterward — score, the holes you converted, and any hole where all four of you missed — and I'll debrief it against this plan.

briefing.focus: 38 rounds of scoring summaries across three seasons. 2024 was your best year by a distance and 2025 gave all of it back — and the one number that has gotten worse every single year, with no exceptions, is your par-5 average.

sections.t: The three cards
sections.b: 2023 · 20 rounds — 5% birdies, 32% pars, 41% bogeys, 20% doubles, 2% triples. Par-or-better 37%. 2024 · 8 rounds — 4% birdies, 39% pars, 43% bogeys, 13% doubles, 1% triples. Par-or-better 43%. 2025 · 10 rounds — 2% birdies, 30% pars, 47% bogeys, 20% doubles, 1% triples. Par-or-better 32%. Read down the par-or-better column and the shape of the three years is obvious: 37 → 43 → 32.

sections.t: THE FINDING — par 5s have gotten worse every year
sections.b: 5.46 → 5.72 → 5.88. That's the only metric on these three cards that moves in one direction with no exceptions, and it has cost you roughly a stroke and a half a round from where it started. On a par-72 with four par 5s, 2023's average gave you +1.8 on them; 2025 gave you +3.5. Par 5s are the holes a mid-single-digit is SUPPOSED to feed on — you get a wedge in your hand on the third shot by design. Instead they've quietly become your worst holes relative to par.

sections.t: It's the same finding Wianno gave you
sections.b: The member-guest cards said it independently: 8 par-5 plays, four pars and four bogeys, ZERO birdies, +4. Two completely different data sources, same conclusion. That's no longer a small-sample fluke — it's the standing pattern, and it's the single most concrete thing on your whole card to attack. The fix is already written down: decide the lay-up off the ladder (PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80) so the third shot is a NUMBER you own rather than whatever's left after hitting it as far as it goes.

sections.t: What actually happened in 2025
sections.b: Bogeys went from 43% to 47% and pars fell from 39% to 30% — that's nine points of pars converting almost one-for-one into bogeys. Doubles also went back up, 13% → 20%. So 2025 wasn't one blow-up round dragging the averages; it was the routine hole getting worse. Rough arithmetic on a par-72 with 4/10/4: 2023 ≈ 86.4, 2024 ≈ 84.2, 2025 ≈ 87.9. Roughly a four-shot swing between your best year and your last one.

sections.t: What 2024 proves you can do
sections.b: Don't dismiss 2024 as a fluke just because it's eight rounds. 39% pars and 13% doubles is genuinely good golf, and the par-4 average — 4.65 — is nearly THREE TENTHS better than either year on either side of it. Ten par 4s a round makes that worth about three strokes on its own. Whatever you were doing in 2024 off the tee and into the green, that's the level, and it's yours; it's two years old, not theoretical.

sections.t: The one thing that held up
sections.b: Par 3s: 3.88 → 3.70 → 3.74. They improved from 2023 and then stayed improved through the bad year. That's a real gain and worth knowing, because it means the collapse in 2025 was not a general ball-striking collapse — one-shot holes held while the two- and three-shot holes fell apart. That points at what happens AFTER the tee shot, not at the swing itself.

sections.t: Read the sample sizes honestly
sections.b: Eight rounds in 2024 against twenty in 2023 — small samples move a lot, and none of these are adjusted for course difficulty, tees played, or conditions. Only two rounds in the whole three years carry GHIN's shot-level detail, so there's no fairways/greens/putts data behind any of this to explain WHY. Treat the year-by-year direction as real and the exact decimals as noisy. What survives that caveat is the par-5 line, because it moves the same way three years running and Wianno confirms it from a separate source.

sections.t: The one job
sections.b: Don't try to fix all of this. Par 5s are the leak with the most evidence behind it, the clearest mechanism, and a fix that's already on your card and costs nothing to apply. Take the ladder number on every par-5 lay-up for the rest of this season and watch that 5.88. Everything else here is context.

PUTTING — First LINK session: lay an alignment stick down the target line and check the toes run PARALLEL, trail foot a touch back. New topline = new sight picture, and the pull left showed up again on the course Jul 29 — that's a stance fault, not a head fault.

PUTTING — Bed in the settled stroke with the LINK.2.1: deep bend / stand close, and the SOFT press moved with the body. Confirm it on one face-on clip — shaft lean at address vs at impact. The stroke does NOT change because the head did.

PUTTING — Film one face-on clip with the LINK.2.1 (shaft lean at impact, where the head bottoms out; also closes early-lift). The 30-ft lag ladder is now live, not parked — it's the top item on the card.

faults.why: THE #1 OPEN FAULT, and the head swap resets it to zero. The Jul 29 round was lags finishing SHORT and short putts running HOT — not two faults but one uncalibrated power curve: too-small a stroke when the number is big, too-big when it's small. The DF3i was convicted after 12 days without one calibrated lag session, so nothing about it was proven. Fix is reps, not hardware: 30-ft lag ladder twice a week, logging spread and how many finish short. Check the LINK's grip first — a grip that isn't the Press Pistol 2° changes shaft lean, loft and therefore pace on its own.

STRENGTHENED Jul 30. The trail foot creeps FORWARD at address, opening the stance line and aiming him LEFT — and in an SBST stroke the shoulder line is the track, so it points the takeaway left too. The pull left reappeared on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in hand while mat blocks ran 10/10 on line: a fault that shows on grass and not on the mat is a setup-and-pressure fault, not a head fault. Trail foot a touch back (square will feel closed), aim the FACE to the spot before building the stance. Re-check aim with a stick on the LINK — new topline, new sight picture.

Confirmed Jul 29, fix chosen the same day: the press was being HELD through the stroke, stacking lean and de-lofting at impact. The fix is a much SOFTER press moved together with the body. Still UNVERIFIED — one face-on clip comparing lean at address vs at impact closes it, and it's now the oldest open item on the card. Extra reason to shoot it: if the LINK came with a different grip, the address lean changed too.

NEW, watch-only. The LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade with far less MOI than the DF3i mallet, so off-centre strikes lose more distance — landing on the one metric already open (pace). Cuts both ways: a blade REPORTS strike quality where a mallet hides it, so it may teach the power curve faster. Judge it off the lag-ladder spread at two weeks. If pace is still scattered with everything else frozen, head weight is the dial to turn — not another putter.

DTL film (Session 8) shows the head staying low and extending down-line — strongly corroborated as gone. One face-on clip closes it, and the press-release check is that same clip: film it in the first LINK session.

metrics.name: Path
metrics.verdict: SETTLED — straight (SBST), confirmed across 20+ clips, three putters, four sessions. Path is yours, not the putter's; the head swap doesn't touch it.

metrics.name: Tempo / load
metrics.verdict: HOLDING — measured 2.4:1 with the DF3i (0.55s/0.23s). Re-measure once on the LINK: a different head weight can quietly change the beat.

metrics.name: Face at impact
metrics.verdict: Square at address and start lines prove it at impact — and the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced like the DF3i, so the design guarantee carries over intact.

metrics.name: Early lift
metrics.verdict: THE OLDEST OPEN ITEM — no angle has re-tested it. One face-on clip in the first LINK session closes the book, and it doubles as the press-release check.

metrics.verdict: REOPENED Jul 30 — clean on every filmed rep and 10/10 in two mat blocks, but a pull LEFT returned on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in hand. That split is the case for the stance leak: it lives on grass and under pressure, where the mat can't see it.

briefing.focus: UPDATED Jul 30 — new head, same routine. The DF3i is out, the L.A.B. LINK.2.1 is in: still zero-torque, just a narrow blade instead of a big mallet. Nothing below changes because of it. Three feels, kept: GET LOW — the deep bend is the anchor. The trigger is a SOFT manual press moved with the body. And the TRAIL FOOT creeps forward, which aims you left — set it a touch back and square will feel closed.

sections.t: THE HEADLINE — get low
sections.b: Your words, and they go at the top of the plan rather than the bottom of a setup list: bending over is the most massive thing, and getting low is where you feel most comfortable. That is the feel to remember when everything else has drifted. If you only carry one thought to the practice green, carry this one — not the press, not the rehearsals, not the pace word. Deep bend, stand close, eyes down.

sections.t: Why the bend is more than comfort
sections.b: Two real mechanisms sit under that feel. FIRST — the LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced, exactly like the DF3i was, and that balance is only true when the shaft is presented at the lie angle it was built for. Stand too tall or too far away and the toe drops, the shaft leaves its designed lie, and the zero-torque property you switched putters for quietly degrades. Posture is what delivers the technology — and that is just as true of the blade as it was of the mallet. It also makes the build spec non-negotiable: your DF3i was 34", set flat. Confirm the LINK is the same before you read anything into how it rolls. SECOND — more bend lets the arms hang freer and tilts the shoulders onto a STEEPER plane, and a steeper shoulder plane is what produces a straight-back-straight-through stroke. Standing tall flattens that plane and builds an arc into the stroke whether you want one or not. Your stroke is SBST on film. The deep bend is the posture that matches it.

sections.t: The setup
sections.b: BEND OVER, stand close, eyes down through the strike. Ball off the LEFT BREAST. Weight stacked ON the ball — pressure over it, not on the trail foot. TRAIL FOOT a touch BACK — it creeps forward on its own and opens you. Hands EVEN with the ball at address; the grip's built-in 2° supplies the lean. ONE CHECK ON THE NEW PUTTER: that rule is a Press Pistol 2° rule. If the LINK didn't come with that grip, your hands-even address no longer produces the same shaft lean, which means the effective loft — and therefore the pace — changed with the grip and not the head. Look at what's on it before you blame anything else. Rock the shoulders, no hands. Loose grip.

sections.t: NEW HEAD — what the routine does about it (nothing)
sections.b: Deliberately nothing. Everything above was built from film of YOUR stroke — path, shoulder plane, stance line, trigger — and none of it was derived from the DF3i's shape. A putter change is not a reason to rebuild a routine; it's a reason to hold the routine still so you can actually see what the putter did. The only two things the swap legitimately touches are the SPEC (length, lie, grip — check them) and your AIM PICTURE (new topline, new sight line — re-check it with a stick). Both are setup checks, not stroke changes. If pace is still erratic after two calibrated sessions with everything else frozen, then it's the head's power curve and we adjust head weight. That's the order.

sections.t: THE TRAIL FOOT — the alignment leak
sections.b: Self-reported Jul 29 and worth taking seriously: your right foot creeps UP — forward, toward the target line — and it drags the stance line open with it. Open the feet and the shoulders follow, so you end up aimed LEFT of where you think you are. The fix is exactly what you said: set that trail foot a touch further back than feels natural. Expect it to feel CLOSED, like you're aimed right. That feeling is the correction, not an error — you're recalibrating off an open baseline, so square will read as closed until it beds in. Trust the line you set, not the feel, for the first few sessions.

sections.t: Why it wrecks the takeaway specifically
sections.b: Because in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track. There's no arc to absorb a misaligned setup — 'straight back' is straight back along whatever line your shoulders are on, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Then one of two things happens, and both are bad: you feel it immediately and manipulate the takeaway to save it, which puts the HANDS back in charge of a stroke built to have no hands in it — or you don't, and the ball starts left. That's why a stance error shows up as a takeaway problem. The takeaway is fine; it's obeying a line that's wrong.

sections.t: This is the miss the putter can't fix
sections.b: Your signature miss is LEFT on short putts — the through-line of the entire putter saga, and it showed up AGAIN on the course Jul 29 with a zero-torque putter in your hands. That is the most useful data point you've generated in weeks, because it rules the head out. A perfectly square face aimed at a target that's left of the hole produces precisely that miss, and no putter ever built will save you from it. Zero-torque guarantees the FACE stays square; it cannot guarantee the face is square TO THE RIGHT THING. Note the split that makes the case: your last two 10-ball blocks started 10/10 on line on the mat, and then you pulled it on grass. Stance creep is a course-and-pressure fault — mat reps are exactly where it wouldn't show. And one thing to redo with the new putter: you changed sight lines. A narrow blade topline frames the target differently from a wide mallet, so re-run the alignment-stick check in your first LINK session and don't assume your aim carried over.

sections.t: The check that costs nothing
sections.b: Lay a club or an alignment stick down the target line just outside the ball on the practice green and set up to it — your toes should run PARALLEL to it, not converging toward it. Ten seconds, and it recalibrates the feel. The structural safeguard is already in your routine: aim the FACE to the spot FIRST, then build the stance around it. Keep that order religiously. If you build the stance first, the face gets aimed to a crooked body; if you aim the face first and the stance then creeps, the mismatch shows up as discomfort — and discomfort you can feel is information you can act on.

sections.t: THE TRIGGER — settled: soft press, moved with the body
sections.b: After cycling through the alternatives you've landed back on a manual forward press — but a genuinely SOFT one, barely doing anything, made in conjunction with the body starting to move. Keep it. That combination is the best version of the hand press there is, and it fixes the exact thing that was wrong on Jul 29. The press isn't doing the LEAN work any more; the grip's 2° does that. It's doing the RHYTHM work. And because the body is moving with it, the press gets carried into the stroke instead of held in place — the release happens on its own rather than being something you have to remember to do.

sections.t: The one rule — softness IS the safeguard
sections.b: A press that small can't stack much lean even if some of it survives to impact, which is precisely why the soft version is safe and the firm one wasn't. So the rule isn't 'press correctly', it's 'keep it tiny'. Two drift signals to watch for: if the press ever starts to feel FIRM, or if it starts to feel like a POSITION you arrive at and sit in rather than a motion you pass through, it has crept back toward the hold. Same size, same softness, every putt — and it still gets its rep at the end of rehearsal 2.

sections.t: If it creeps back into a hold
sections.b: The alternatives stay on the shelf rather than getting deleted, because you may want one later: THE FLOAT — lift the head a hair off the turf before takeaway; no hand action at all and it removes ground friction. THE WHOLE-PUTTER WAGGLE — small forward-and-back from the shoulders, wrists silent. THE LEAD-SHOULDER SETTLE — a soft downward press of the shoulder that already runs the stroke. THE TRAIL-KNEE KICK — furthest from the hands, and the same trigger your full-swing routine uses. Any of them will break inertia without the hands touching shaft lean. You don't need one right now.

sections.t: How to tell it's releasing
sections.b: One face-on clip settles it: compare shaft lean at ADDRESS with shaft lean at IMPACT. Close to equal means the soft press is passing through the way it should. Meaningfully more at impact means it's being carried in, whatever it felt like — and feel is exactly what got this wrong the first time. The free check needs no camera: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click, a ball driven down into the green adds a faint scuff a beat later. Listen for the scuff.

sections.t: Stop shopping
sections.b: Straight talk, because you called it yourself. That's three putters in a month, and the DF3i got 12 days and not one calibrated lag session before you convicted it. Twelve days isn't enough to convict a putter — it's enough to convict a power curve you never built. The swap itself is defensible: you kept zero-torque and you changed shape, which is a real preference and not a mistake. What isn't survivable is doing it again in two weeks. So the LINK gets a gate: two weeks, a 20-ball 5-footer test and a 30-foot lag ladder each week, and the verdict comes off those numbers rather than off an afternoon's feel. Keep the DF3i in the bullpen until then — don't sell it. And keep the stroke frozen while the head is the variable: the deep bend and the soft press were both decided from clear feel and both are mechanically sound. One variable at a time.

sections.t: Why beside the ball and not behind it
sections.b: Rehearsing in your true putting posture — same deep bend, same arm hang, same shoulder plane — means the stroke that FEELS like 30 feet is the stroke you actually make. Magnitude transfers one-to-one. Rehearsing from behind the ball reads the break better, but you're standing upright there, so the size you feel is only an approximation. Your open fault is pace magnitude, not reading: path ✓, face ✓, start lines 10/10 twice over. Optimise the thing that's broken.

sections.t: Keep the order of the two rehearsals
sections.b: Ball-look first (path and contact), hole-look second (pace). The last thing you feel is the thing you carry in — so the pace stroke must be the last one. If the hole stroke ever drifts to first, the pace feel gets overwritten by the contact feel and you're back to guessing distance. Finish rehearsal 2 WITH the soft press, at its real size: it's the one part of the stroke that never used to get a practice rep, which is how it drifted last time without you noticing.

sections.t: Two rules underneath it
sections.b: SAME BEAT COUNT, EVERY PUTT — a routine that varies in length is itself a pace variable, and the putts where you take an extra look are the ones that come up short. And a VERBAL BACKSTOP is worth testing: say the pace intention right before the press ('die it a foot past', 'back of the cup'). Feel decays, a word doesn't.

sections.t: Still to test — lags
sections.b: This is no longer a someday item — it's the top of the card. Yesterday's round was lags coming up SHORT and short putts running HOT, which is not two faults but one: a power curve you haven't learned, so you under-hit the long ones and over-hit the short ones. A new head resets that curve to zero, so the reps have to be deliberate. The block test, twice a week: 10 balls from 30 feet, and measure the SPREAD of stopping points plus how many finish short. Then the experiment worth running while you're there — past ~25 feet, keep your eyes ON THE HOLE through the actual stroke, not just the rehearsal. Feels absurd, works well; the ball isn't moving, you don't need to watch it. 10 eyes-on-ball vs 10 eyes-on-hole, same session, compare the spreads.

Rehearsal 2 — eyes on the HOLE. Pace. Finish it with the soft press.

Spot → ball → soft press with the body → putt

briefing.course: The LINK.2.1 Swap — What Changes, What Travels
briefing.focus: Jul 30. DF3i out, L.A.B. LINK.2.1 in, after a round of short lags, hot short putts and a pull left. What the new head genuinely changes, what follows you across any putter, and the two-week gate that ends the shopping.

sections.t: First — this is a legal move
sections.b: You didn't undo the fix. The LINK.2.1 is Lie Angle Balanced — the same zero-torque technology as the DF3i, in L.A.B.'s narrow-body heel-shafted blade. The thing that made the Phantom 7.5 wrong for you (toe flow fighting a straight-back-straight-through stroke) is still absent from your bag. So this is a SHAPE change, not a technology change, and it doesn't reopen the mismatch that started this whole saga. Worth saying clearly because it looks like a step back toward a blade: it isn't. You've got the blade LOOK you've always been drawn to sitting on top of the mechanics your stroke actually needs. That's about the best outcome available here.

sections.t: "It felt like a lot" is real information
sections.b: The DF3i is a wide, deep, high-MOI mallet. The LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade. That's a large change in what sits behind the ball, and it changes the sight line, the perceived weight, and how much the head seems to be asking for. Don't apologise for it or file it under 'being crazy' — putter feel drives COMMITMENT, and commitment is worth measurable strokes on short putts. A putter you trust at address is not a soft consideration. The mistake would be acting on feel and then never measuring; the feel itself is fine.

sections.t: What you gave up — and it lands on your open fault
sections.b: Forgiveness. A narrow blade has far less MOI than that mallet, so off-centre strikes lose more distance than they used to. Your one remaining open fault is PACE. So you've moved to a head that is less tolerant of exactly the thing you're already struggling with, and you should know that going in. The counter-argument is real too: a forgiving head HIDES strike quality, a blade reports it. If your contact is good, the blade will teach you its power curve faster and give you better feedback while you learn. If your contact is patchy, it'll cost you distance control. Which one is true for you is an empirical question, and the gate below answers it.

sections.t: Yesterday's round, read properly
sections.b: Lags finishing SHORT and short putts BLOWN BY look like two contradictory faults. They're one. It's the signature of an uncalibrated power curve: with no reliable mapping from stroke size to distance, you default to too-small when the number is big and too-big when the number is small — and both errors show up in the same round. That is not a defect in the DF3i. It's what 12 days with any new head looks like when none of those days included a lag session. The lesson transfers directly: the LINK will have its own curve, and you'll get the same round again unless you build it deliberately.

sections.t: The pull left travels with you
sections.b: The left miss appeared again on the course while you were holding a zero-torque putter. That's the cleanest evidence yet that the head was never the cause. It points at the alignment leak already on your card: the trail foot creeping forward, opening the stance line, aiming you left — and in an SBST stroke the shoulder line IS the track, so an open stance doesn't just aim you left, it points the whole stroke left. Zero-torque protects the face; it can't protect where the face is pointing. Trail foot a touch back, aim the FACE to the spot before you build the stance, and expect square to feel closed for a few sessions.

sections.t: The one spec that must be right
sections.b: Lie Angle Balanced is only TRUE at the length and lie the putter was built for — that's not marketing, it's the whole mechanism. Your DF3i was 34" and set flat. If the LINK is a stock pull-off-the-rack build, get its numbers and match them, because a putter that's a degree or two off your fitted lie is a putter whose headline technology is partly switched off. Second check, and this one could explain your pace on its own: THE GRIP. Your entire setup rule is 'hands even with the ball, the grip's 2° supplies the lean' — that's a Press Pistol 2° rule. Different grip, different shaft lean at address, different effective loft, different roll and different distance for the same stroke. Confirm what's on the LINK before you draw a single conclusion about how it rolls.

sections.t: Head weight is the adjustable variable — later
sections.b: L.A.B. builds static head weight to the putter's length, and a blade generally carries a different weight from a mallet. Head weight is the most direct lever on distance control there is: a heavier head produces a shorter, more repeatable stroke for a given distance, which usually helps lag control; a lighter head asks for a longer stroke and gives more feel on short ones. If pace is still scattered after two properly calibrated weeks, this is the dial to turn — and it's a cheap change compared to another putter. But don't touch it before you have baseline numbers, or you'll be changing two things at once and learn nothing.

sections.t: THE GATE — how the LINK gets judged
sections.b: Two weeks, then a verdict on numbers rather than on an afternoon. (1) THE 20-BALL 5-FOOTER, once a week, logged in the Putting Lab with miss directions — the pass mark is the same one the grip experiment used: 2 or fewer LEFT misses per 20. That tests aim and face, not the head. (2) THE 30-FOOT LAG LADDER, twice a week: 10 balls, and record two things — the SPREAD of stopping points and how many finished SHORT. Short is the fault to kill; a ball that finishes two feet past is a made putt that missed, a ball that finishes two feet short was never in. (3) ONE FACE-ON CLIP in the first session — it closes the early-lift fault and checks the soft press is releasing, and it's now the oldest open item on your card.

sections.t: No fourth head without evidence
sections.b: Keep the DF3i in the bullpen — don't sell it while the LINK is unproven. Hold the stroke exactly where it is: the deep bend and the soft press were both decided from clear feel in the last week and both are mechanically sound, so freezing them is what makes the head readable as a variable. And if the LINK's numbers at two weeks aren't better than the DF3i's, the conclusion is NOT a fourth putter. It's that pace is a reps-and-calibration problem that was never going to be solved by hardware — at which point the cheapest fix on the board is the lag ladder you already own.
