briefing.focus: You feel better with the weight BACK while the ball sits off the front foot — and you've heard the weight is supposed to be forward. Here's what that combination actually costs you, why it lands squarely on the one putting fault still open on your card, and how to settle it with evidence instead of dogma. UPDATED Jul 30 for the LINK.2.1: the blade has far less MOI than the DF3i mallet, so a wandering low point now costs real distance — everything below matters more, not less.

sections.t: What 'weight forward' is actually for
sections.b: It isn't a rule for its own sake. Lead-side pressure does one job: it PINS THE LOW POINT of the stroke. Where your weight sits decides where the arc bottoms out, and where the arc bottoms out decides how the LINK.2.1 meets the ball. That's the whole mechanism — everything below follows from it.

sections.t: The cost — loft, hop, skid, short
sections.b: Ball off the FRONT foot is correct. But weight back moves the bottom of the arc BEHIND the ball, so by the time the putter arrives the head is climbing hard and the shaft is leaning AWAY from the target. That adds loft you never asked for. The ball launches slightly, HOPS, SKIDS, and only then starts rolling. Every bit of that hop is energy that was supposed to become roll — so the putt arrives soft. Worse, the skid distance changes with green speed and grain, so your PACE stops being repeatable from green to green.

sections.t: Why this is your fault, specifically
sections.b: Read the card. Path: settled. Face: settled. Start line: 10/10 clean, twice over. The ONE thing still open is pace — lags coming up short at Hudson Hills, arrivals dying on the mat, and both genuine misses in the Stage-0 4-footer block DIED at the hole. Hop-and-skid off a back-weighted low point is the textbook cause of exactly that signature. Your stroke is no longer the problem. Your strike quality might be.

sections.t: The second cost — the pull
sections.b: Sitting back drops the trail shoulder and slides your EYELINE behind the ball. Eyes behind the ball make you see the line right of where it truly is, and you square it up with a whisker of pull. Both real misses in the Stage-0 block settled on the PULL side — logged there as a lean, not proof. This belongs on that candidate-cause list.

sections.t: The third cost — the flip can come back
sections.b: Hanging back leaves the hands behind the ball through impact. Hands behind = the wrists want to save it = a flick. That flick was the engine of the old blow-through left miss. The LINK.2.1's zero-torque head has buried that miss on film — but hands-behind is the one setup that can wake it up.

sections.t: Before changing anything — feel isn't real
sections.b: Your own Golf Mind note states the principle: 'Hands over the ball: it FEELS like a forward press, but it isn't.' The same illusion runs in reverse. Weight that FEELS back is often pressure that's actually close to neutral — and neutral may be perfectly fine. Don't discard a setup you putt well from on the strength of a feel. FILM IT FACE-ON first. That single clip also closes the early-lift fault, the last open item from Session 8.

sections.t: What has to be true (the real checklist)
sections.b: Forget 'weight forward' as a slogan. Four things actually matter, and you can keep your comfort as long as they hold. (1) STERNUM at or just ahead of the ball. (2) HANDS level with or a touch ahead of the ball at impact — never behind it. (3) LOW POINT at or just behind the ball, so the LINK.2.1 is a HAIR ascending at contact — that slight upstroke is what produces true roll. (4) PRESSURE around 55/45 lead — enough to anchor the low point, not so much that you start steering. If your weight-back feel still delivers 1 through 3, keep it.

sections.t: One thing in your favor
sections.b: This section used to say the head would cover for you. On the LINK.2.1 it won't, and that's the honest update. The DF3i was a wide, heavy mallet — high MOI, self-squaring, happy to be swung rather than steered, and forgiving of a low point that wandered. The LINK.2.1 is a narrow blade: same zero-torque Lie Angle Balanced technology, so the FACE is still protected, but far less MOI, so a strike off the middle bleeds more distance than it used to. That doesn't change a single instruction above — it raises the stakes on all of them. Low point pinned at or just behind the ball, hands never behind it: on a mallet those were worth a little consistency, on a blade they're worth the difference between a lag that finishes and one that dies four feet short. The flip side is genuinely useful: a blade REPORTS a bad strike where a mallet muffles it, so this putter will tell you fast whether your low point is where you think it is. Listen to it.

sections.t: Settle it with data
sections.b: A/B LAG LADDER — 30 feet, two blocks of 10. Block A: your current feel. Block B: the change you're testing, everything else identical. Mark where each ball STOPS and measure the spread. Tighter spread wins — that's the answer, not anyone's opinion. SOUND TEST: a purely rolling ball makes one clean click; a hopping ball adds a faint scuff a beat later — listen for the scuff. FACE-ON CLIP: check shaft lean at impact and where the head bottoms out relative to the ball. Note the weight question itself is already settled on the mat (ball off the left breast, weight stacked ON the ball) — this ladder is here as the measuring protocol for any future change, not an open question. One amendment as of Jul 30: the head changed, so the A/B is now the FIRST thing that gets run on the LINK.2.1 rather than a follow-up — you're building this putter's power curve from scratch anyway, and you may as well build it with the low point in the right place instead of calibrating around a fault.

briefing.focus: Scramble, not stroke play. Your job is to be the team's SECOND ball — when someone's already safe, swing free and go at the flag. And on every lay-up, leave the team one of YOUR numbers (122 · 108 · 95 · 80), never a 70-yard guess. First round with the LINK.2.1 — treat every early putt as free calibration.

sections.t: The course in one paragraph
sections.b: Beekman Golf Course, Hopewell Junction NY (11 Country Club Rd) — a 1964 Cortlandt Fish public 27-holer in the Berkshire foothills where they rise out of the Hudson Valley, about an hour's drive for you. Three nines — HIGHLAND (3,142 yds, par 36, ~124 slope), VALLEY (2,952, par 35, ~118), TACONIC (3,125, par 36, ~126) — played in three 18-hole pairings between 6,485 and 6,532 yards. Zoysia fairways, which is the detail worth knowing: zoysia sits the ball UP on a tight, firm cushion, so contact is clean and there's less grab than the bent/poa you're used to. Reviews are consistent — well-kept greens, all three nines hilly, and it doesn't drain well, so wet spots after rain.

sections.t: Find out which two nines you're playing
sections.b: Ask at check-in, because the three nines are genuinely different golf courses. TACONIC is the hardest: narrowest fairways and the water — the par-5 6th has a pond fronting the green, which in a scramble is a decision hole, not a hero hole. HIGHLAND climbs over 500 feet to a panorama of Stormville Mountain: elevation change on nearly every shot, blind or semi-blind looks, and the yardage on the sprinkler head is a starting point, not the answer. VALLEY is the gentlest and flattest of the three — that's your birdie nine, and a scramble team that only pars the Valley holes has already lost the tournament.

sections.t: Scramble math — where teams actually win
sections.b: You don't win a scramble by avoiding doubles; the format erases those for you. You win it by converting the 5–7 genuinely gettable holes and by never wasting a hole where all four of you miss. So the whole game is about SEQUENCING: get one ball safe, then let everyone else be aggressive off that safety net. The single biggest error you'll see all day is the team's last hitter playing conservatively when a ball is already in the fairway — that shot is completely free, and a free shot played safe is a shot thrown away.

sections.t: Your role off the tee
sections.b: You have the perfect scramble bag for this: mini driver (~220) and the KING TEC 2-iron (~205) for when a ball simply has to be in the short grass, and the Stealth 2 for when one already is. Rule for the day: if nobody is safe yet, hit the club you'd bet $100 finds the fairway — on Taconic's tight holes and Highland's blind ones, that's the mini or the 2-iron, and nobody on your team will ever complain about a ball in play. If someone IS safe, take the driver and take the whole thing on. Your own note from the swing plan applies double here: the straight one comes from a LONGER, fuller swing; steering it is what turns it into the push-slice. In a scramble you have permission to make the fullest swing you own.

sections.t: Approaches — the lay-up is the shot that scores
sections.b: This is the biggest edge you personally bring, and almost nobody uses it. In a scramble you CHOOSE the yardage for the next shot. On any par 5 you're laying up on — including Taconic's 6th over the water — pick the ball that leaves a full 95 (56°) or a full 108 (50°), not the one that's 18 yards closer and leaves a nervy three-quarter 70-yarder. Same on a punch-out. Your ladder off the 44° PW: PW 122 · 50° 108 · 56° 95 · 60° 80. Say the number out loud when the team is choosing the ball — it's the most useful sentence you can contribute all day. On approaches themselves: first player in plays to the CENTER of the green, everyone after that fires at the flag. Uphill into these hillside greens, club UP; anything short rolls back down to you.

sections.t: The hill, the lies, and your free club-length
sections.b: All three nines are hilly, so you'll get very few flat lies — except that a scramble hands you a club-length of relief (confirm no-closer-to-the-hole at check-in). USE IT properly: don't just drop it where it's convenient, walk it to the flattest stance and the best ANGLE into the flag, and get out of any divot or wet spot. When you're stuck with a slope: ball above your feet turns it LEFT — with your strong lofts take one less and aim at the right edge; ball below the feet leaks right, so widen the stance and swing smooth. On the Highland especially, trust the elevation over the number.

sections.t: Putting — the whole team's read is yours to use
sections.b: Best sequencing: whoever's least confident putts first and the best putter goes last, so the last ball has watched three balls take the line. Everyone marks the spot and putts from it. Two things that win scrambles on the green: the early putters should get the ball PAST the hole so the team learns the break and the speed — a putt left short teaches nothing — and the last putter plays the read that the first three just paid for. For you specifically — and note this is your FIRST round with the LINK.2.1, two days after the swap: the putter still handles the face (it's zero-torque, same as the DF3i), so your job is pace, and pace is exactly what you haven't calibrated on this head yet. A scramble is the perfect place to learn it at zero cost — you're often putting after someone's already safe, so roll the early ones firmly PAST and let the misses teach you the new power curve, and the routine still runs on every putt, including the 3-footer after a teammate has already stuffed it close. Your signature miss is left on the short ones, and 'gimme' tap-ins in a scramble are exactly where a stroke gets loose.

sections.t: The opening hole — you have data on this
sections.b: Wianno told you the truth in numbers: across five opening holes you went 6, 6, 5, 4, 6 — SEVEN over par on five holes, and never a par on the first hole of a front nine. That's a not-warmed-up problem, not a swing problem, and you're driving an hour to a 7 AM-ish start. Get there early enough for the warm-up primer off the swing plan: a few slow ONE-HANDED reps (Miracle 201 or trail-arm-only), feeling the trail elbow lead down into the slot, then blend to two-handed swings. Then five minutes on the putting green for pace only — zoysia surrounds and well-kept greens mean you want the speed calibrated before the first putt counts for four people.

sections.t: Confirm these at check-in
sections.b: Scramble formats vary and the details change your strategy: (1) is there a MINIMUM DRIVES rule — most events require each player's tee shot be used two or three times? If so, bank yours early on the wide holes rather than discovering on 17 that you owe two. (2) Net or gross, and how team handicap is figured. (3) Whether they're selling mulligans/skins — buy them for the tightest tee shots, not the first hole. (4) Cart path only? On a course this hilly, that changes club selection every hole. (5) Which nines, and shotgun or tee times.

sections.t: Mindset for the day
sections.b: Early August, hilly, an hour in the car first — take the cart, drink more than you think, and load the weather tile at the first tee so the ladder's Today column adjusts your carries for the heat. This is the one round all year where your worst shot literally does not exist, so the risk-management instincts that serve you in stroke play are mostly wrong here: be the guy who takes on the flag once a teammate is safe. Log it in Coach afterward — score, the holes you converted, and any hole where all four of you missed — and I'll debrief it against this plan.

entries.setup: 8 clips · 3× overhead + 5× ground-level DTL · L.A.B. LINK.2.1 — first filmed reps · lined return mat
entries.finding: Tempo 2.0:1 across 7 of 8 clips ✓. Path straight (SBST) ✓. Stance measured SQUARE to slightly closed — the trail-foot creep is FIXED ✓. But 2 of 3 overhead putts started 1.5–1.7° LEFT (1.3–1.4" left at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft); the third was dead straight. Path is neutral, so the face was left at impact on those two — aimed there, or closed on the way through. Feet are ruled out; the leak has moved up to the face or the shoulders.

metrics.n: ¼–½" inside at the top, back on line by impact

detail.story:
Eight clips, two angles, first filmed reps with the LINK.2.1 — three overhead (the gold-standard angle for path and start line) and five ground-level down-the-line. Measured frame by frame against the mat's own printed lines, with the ball's 1.68" diameter as the ruler.

THE MACHINERY IS GOOD. Tempo came out at 2.0 : 1 — seven of the eight clips landed between 1.9 and 2.1, one outlier at 1.6. That is tour-window and it is repeatable, measured two independent ways (head travel overhead, apparent head size down-the-line) that agreed with each other. Path is straight: the head worked a quarter to a half inch inside on the backstroke and was back on the line by impact — that is SBST, confirmed again, and the new head hasn't disturbed it. Stroke shape was 7–8 inches back and 15–16 inches through, a strongly accelerating stroke.

AND THE STANCE IS NOT THE PROBLEM. Your feet are visible in the overhead frames, so the trail-foot creep — the prime suspect on the card since Jul 29 — got measured directly for the first time. The toe line came out 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED relative to the target line across the three putts. Never open, not once. You fixed that. If anything you have over-corrected a touch, which is the expected overshoot when 'square feels closed'.

BUT THE BALL STILL STARTED LEFT. Two of the three overhead putts left the face 1.5° and 1.7° left of the mat's centre line — that is 1.3 and 1.4 inches left of target at 4 feet, and about 2 inches at 6 feet. The third was dead straight (0.2°). The control matters here: all three were shot from the same fixed camera and run through the same measurement, and one of them showed zero drift, so the left reading on the other two is real and not an artefact of the method.

WHAT THAT MEANS. On a putt, start direction is dominated by the face, not the path — and your path measured neutral. So on those two putts the face was pointing left at impact. There are only two ways that happens: the face was AIMED left at address, or it CLOSED on the way through. Your feet are now ruled out as the cause, so if it is aim, the leak has moved UP — to the face itself, or to the shoulder line. And the fact that one putt of three was perfect says this is variability, not a fixed bias baked into the setup.

This is your signature miss — left on short putts — appearing on film for the first time since the switch to zero-torque. Worth saying plainly: it is not the putter. It happened with the DF3i on the course Jul 29 and it is happening with the LINK.2.1 on the mat now. Two different zero-torque heads, same miss. The head was never the variable.
detail.compare: Session 5 (DF3i, overhead) had 5 of 5 balls starting dead on the centre line, and two 10-ball mat blocks ran 10/10 on line. Those were eyeball reads of whether the ball looked on line; this is the first time the start line has been MEASURED in degrees, and at 1.5° the drift is small enough that it would have looked fine on those earlier clips — 1.3" at 4 feet still finds the middle of a 4.25" hole. That is why it never showed on the mat and did show on the course: at 4 feet it is a make, at 6 feet it is an edge, at 10 feet it is a miss. Tempo is the other continuity — 2.4:1 measured in Session 5 with the DF3i, 2.0:1 now with the LINK. Both inside the window; the blade may simply want a slightly quicker transition.
detail.limits: Neither angle can see shaft lean, so the held-press question is still open and the early-lift fault still has no verdict — both need ONE face-on clip, which is now the oldest item on your card and the single most valuable thing you can film. Face-on is also what separates the two remaining explanations for the left start: aimed left at address versus closing through impact. The overhead can measure your feet but not your shoulders — your upper body is out of frame — so shoulder alignment is unmeasured. And every one of these was a flat mat rep: nothing here says anything about pace, which is still the fault with the least evidence against it.

metrics.verdict: THE FAULT, now measured. 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT on two of three overhead putts — 1.3–1.4" left at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft — with one dead straight. Small enough to hide on the mat, big enough to miss from 6 feet out. Exactly the signature miss.

faults.why: MEASURED Jul 30, and now the number-one fault. Two of three overhead putts started 1.5° and 1.7° LEFT of the mat's centre line — 1.3–1.4" left at 4 ft, ~2" at 6 ft — while the third was dead straight. Path measured neutral, and start direction on a putt is dominated by the face, so the face was pointing left at impact. Two candidates remain and only ONE face-on clip separates them: the face was AIMED left at address, or it CLOSED through impact. Note it happened with the DF3i on grass and the LINK.2.1 on the mat — two zero-torque heads, same miss. This is not the putter.

Still UNVERIFIED and now the blocker. The Jul 29 fix — a much softer press moved with the body — has never been checked, because neither the overhead nor the down-the-line angle can see shaft lean. It matters more than it did: a press that is still being HELD delivers a de-lofted, closed-ish face, which is one of the two live explanations for the left start line above. One face-on clip, lean at address vs lean at impact.

Untouched by this session — every clip was a flat mat rep with no lag work, so nothing here counts as evidence either way. Still the fault with the least data against it, and the LINK.2.1's power curve is still unbuilt. 30-ft lag ladder twice a week, logging spread and how many finish SHORT.

Watch-only, unchanged. The LINK.2.1's narrow blade has far less MOI than the DF3i mallet, so off-centre strikes cost more distance. Judge it off the lag-ladder spread at the two-week gate, not off feel.

CLOSED Jul 30 ✓ — measured, not assumed. The overhead frames show your feet, and the toe line ran 0.6°, 2.9° and 3.6° CLOSED to the target line across three reps. Never open. The trail-foot fix worked, and you may even be a touch past square. Keep setting it where you're setting it; the aim leak, if there is one, is now above the feet — face aim or shoulder line.

entries.text: PUTTING — ONE FACE-ON CLIP. It is now the only thing standing between you and a diagnosis: it separates 'face aimed left' from 'face closing through impact', closes the held-press question (lean at address vs at impact) and closes early-lift. Camera at ball height, square to the target line, 2–3 strokes.

PUTTING — Aim check above the feet. Your stance measured SQUARE on film, so the left start line isn't coming from your feet. Set up to an alignment stick, have someone lay a second club across your SHOULDERS, and check the face against the line with a mirror or a phone from directly above the ball.

PUTTING — The 30-ft LAG LADDER, twice a week: 10 balls, log the SPREAD of stopping points and how many finish SHORT. This is the LINK.2.1's power curve and it's the only fault with no evidence either way. (Face-on filming is now its own item.)

entries.setup: 5 clips · target-side down-the-line (camera on the mat at the hole end, looking back) · L.A.B. LINK.2.1
entries.finding: Posture confirmed — the deep bend is real and repeatable. Lie presentation measured ~22° from vertical (≈68° lie), right where L.A.B. builds these, so the Lie Angle Balanced tech is being delivered by the setup rather than defeated by it. BUT this angle looks ALONG the target line, so it still cannot see shaft lean: the held-press question, the early-lift verdict and the aim-vs-closing-face question are all still open. Face-on is the only angle that closes them.

detail.story:
Five clips from the hole end of the mat looking back up the line. Worth logging what this angle settles and what it can't, so it doesn't get shot again expecting a different answer.

WHAT IT CONFIRMS. The deep bend is genuinely there — torso well forward from the hips, head out over the ball, arms hanging. That's the anchor feel from the locked routine, and it's being executed, not just written down. And the putter is being presented at about 22° from vertical, which works out to roughly a 68° lie — exactly the window L.A.B. builds these in. That matters more than it sounds: Lie Angle Balanced is only TRUE at the lie the putter was built for, and standing it up would quietly switch off the zero-torque property you changed putters to get. It isn't being switched off. Measured across 14 address frames on the one clip that gave a clean fit, the reading was rock steady (±0.1°), so the presentation is repeatable too.

WHY IT CAN'T ANSWER THE OPEN QUESTION. Shaft lean is a tilt toward the target — it lives in the vertical plane that CONTAINS the target line. This camera sits on that same line and looks straight down it, so lean points directly at the lens and projects to nothing. It is the same blind spot the ground-level down-the-line clips have, just from the opposite end. No amount of resolution fixes it; it's the axis that's wrong.

So the three questions that were open this morning are still open: is the press releasing or being held, is early lift gone, and — the big one — is the face AIMED left at address or CLOSING through impact. All three are answered by one clip shot from the SIDE.
detail.limits: Beyond shaft lean: eye position over the line and shoulder alignment were both attempted from this angle and neither survived the error budget. Locating a point 'directly above the target line' from here depends on the mat's lines converging to a vanishing point, and across the five clips that point landed anywhere in a 60-pixel band — about four inches at his distance from the camera. That is far too coarse to call a two-inch eye offset, so nothing is claimed about either. Shoulder line remains the untested suspect now that the feet have been cleared.
